newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Geneva court acquits Nigerian activist of theft.
newsitem.headline: Geneva court acquits Nigerian activist of theft.

text.p: A Geneva criminal court on Friday acquitted a leading Nigerian human rights activist of theft, overturning a recent conviction and ruling there was no proof he stole two women's designer suits.

Clement Nwankwo, a lawyer who heads the Constitutional Rights Project in Nigeria, was in the Swiss city in April to attend the U.N. Commission on Human Rights when he was arrested and sentenced to 20 days in jail. He denied the charges.
The ladies' suits from the boutique Anita Smaga, valued at 2,580 Swiss francs ($1,800) were never found, leading the court to rule on Friday he should be given the benefit of the doubt.

The incident embarrassed the host Swiss delegation to the annual U.N. human rights forum after Nwankwo claimed he was beaten and tortured by Geneva police. Held incommunicado in jail for four days before being swiftly sentenced, he then appealed.

Police, who arrested him when saleswomen reported the suits missing after he had been briefly in the chic shop, argued that physical force had been necessary to restrain him. They denied his charge that he had been beaten or handcuffed naked to a bed.
"He has been acquitted of theft but the court confirmed his conviction for resisting arrest," his lawyer, Olivier Cramer told Reuters. "It is a victory, but not a total one."
The court lifted the three-year expulsion order but kept a four-day sentence for his resisting arrest. This equalled time served in detention so there is no more time to be served.
But his client expected to appeal the sentence for resisting arrest before a higher criminal court, according to Cramer.
Nwankwo, now back in Nigeria, testified he feared being kidnapped when police stopped him at a time when 30 Nigerian government officials were in Geneva for the rights forum.
Days later, the 53-member body appointed its first special investigator to look into allegations of major rights abuses in Nigeria including arbitrary detentions and executions.
